items.title: 6 Critical F5 BIG-IP Vulnerabilities Could Let Hackers Disrupt Websites and Execute Malicious Code
items.summary: F5 released emergency fixes for six critical BIG-IP vulnerabilities that could let remote attackers take websites and other services offline without logging in. The flaws affect specific traffic-handling configurations. An attacker who can reach a vulnerable service could crash the BIG-IP process that handles client traffic. F5 also warned that attackers may be able to run code on affected devices. The company disclosed the flaws in its November 18 out-of-band security notification . The advisory said no exploitation had been reported at the time. That sets this disclosure apart from the BIG-IP OAuth zero-day reported in September , which F5 said attackers were already exploiting. BIG-IP Flaws Take Websites Offline BIG-IP often sits between users and the servers that host a website. Its Traffic Management Microkernel, or TMM, handles connections passing through the device. If that process crashes, users can lose access even when the web servers behind it are still running. The impact is not limited to websites. Remote access portals and other applications that rely on the same device can also become unavailable. These are data-plane flaws, meaning they affect the part of BIG-IP that handles live traffic rather than the interface administrators use to manage it. Keeping the management interface off the internet does not fix the problem if an affected service is still reachable. The result can look similar to an outage caused by the earlier BIG-IP HTTP/2 denial-of-service flaw , but the new flaws involve memory corruption rather than exhaustion of processing power. BIG-IP Deployments Affected Five of the six flaws affect iRules, the scripts administrators use to control how BIG-IP handles traffic. They are CVE-2026-120285, CVE-2026-120292, CVE-2026-116953, CVE-2026-120722 and CVE-2026-121805. Some also affect BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes or BIG-IP Cloud-Native Network Functions. Teams should check the advisory for each flaw against the product and configuration they actually run. The sixth flaw, CVE-2026-123637 , affects BIG-IP Access Policy Manager when a virtual server uses a per-request policy with both the Client Information and Endpoint Security agents. A separate single sign-on flaw, CVE-2026-126822, can also cause an outage without a login, but it is rated high severity and is not part of the six critical issues. F5’s engineering hotfix guide covers BIG-IP TMOS 17.1.x, 17.5.x and 21.1.x. The correct package depends on the exact base release or engineering build already installed. Affected product Versions known to be vulnerable Patched build BIG-IP, including APM, DNS and PEM where listed in the CVE advisory 17.1.0–17.1.3 BIGIP-17.1.3.7.0.21.4-ENG for base releases. Use BIGIP-17.1.3.6.0.14.20-ENG if running BIGIP-17.1.3.6.0.9.20-ENG . BIG-IP, including APM, DNS and PEM where listed in the CVE advisory 17.5.0–17.5.1 BIGIP-17.5.1.11.0.61.12-ENG for base releases. Use BIGIP-17.5.1.10.0.80.35-ENG if running BIGIP-17.5.1.10.0.7.35-ENG or BIG-IP-17.5.1.10.0.37.35-ENG . BIG-IP, including APM, DNS and PEM where listed in the CVE advisory 21.1.0 BIGIP-21.1.0.4.0.19.3-ENG . BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes 2.2.0–2.2.5 2.3.0–2.3.4 2.4.0–2.4.2 BNK-2.2.5-EHF1 BNK-2.3.4-EHF1 BNK-2.4.2-EHF1 BIG-IP Cloud-Native Network Functions (CNF) 2.2.0–2.2.5 2.3.0–2.3.4 2.4.0–2.4.2 CNF-2.2.5-EHF1 CNF-2.3.4-EHF1 CNF-2.4.2-EHF1 For example, a device on the 17.5.1.11 base release should use Hotfix-BIGIP-17.5.1.11.0.61.12-ENG . Devices running either of the two 17.5.1.10 engineering builds named in the guide need Hotfix-BIGIP-17.5.1.10.0.80.35-ENG instead. Customers running a custom build should contact F5 Support for a replacement. F5 lists no workaround for the six critical flaws. Start with internet-facing virtual servers and those that carry traffic for critical services. Record the full installed build before choosing a package, then test the update outside production where possible. After deployment, verify that users can reach the websites and remote access portals served by BIG-IP. F5 released emergency fixes for six critical BIG-IP vulnerabilities that could let remote attackers take websites and other services offline without logging in. The flaws affect specific traffic-handling configurations.

An attacker who can reach a vulnerable service could crash the BIG-IP process that handles client traffic. F5 also warned that attackers may be able to run code on affected devices. The company disclosed the flaws in its November 18 out-of-band security notification.

The advisory said no exploitation had been reported at the time. That sets this disclosure apart from the BIG-IP OAuth zero-day reported in September, which F5 said attackers were already exploiting.

BIG-IP Flaws Take Websites Offline

BIG-IP often sits between users and the servers that host a website. Its Traffic Management Microkernel, or TMM, handles connections passing through the device. If that process crashes, users can lose access even when the web servers behind it are still running.

The impact is not limited to websites. Remote access portals and other applications that rely on the same device can also become unavailable.

These are data-plane flaws, meaning they affect the part of BIG-IP that handles live traffic rather than the interface administrators use to manage it. Keeping the management interface off the internet does not fix the problem if an affected service is still reachable.

The result can look similar to an outage caused by the earlier BIG-IP HTTP/2 denial-of-service flaw, but the new flaws involve memory corruption rather than exhaustion of processing power.

BIG-IP Deployments Affected

Five of the six flaws affect iRules, the scripts administrators use to control how BIG-IP handles traffic. They are CVE-2026-120285, CVE-2026-120292, CVE-2026-116953, CVE-2026-120722 and CVE-2026-121805.

Some also affect BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes or BIG-IP Cloud-Native Network Functions. Teams should check the advisory for each flaw against the product and configuration they actually run.

The sixth flaw, CVE-2026-123637, affects BIG-IP Access Policy Manager when a virtual server uses a per-request policy with both the Client Information and Endpoint Security agents. A separate single sign-on flaw, CVE-2026-126822, can also cause an outage without a login, but it is rated high severity and is not part of the six critical issues.

items.title: WhatsApp Android Flaws Could Let Hackers Delete Users’ Files and Expose IP Addresses
items.summary: WhatsApp’s November 2026 security update describes three flaws that could let attackers delete files stored by WhatsApp on Android, expose a user’s IP address, or bypass a security check for Meta AI’s Private Processing service. Of the three, only the IP exposure flaw was flagged for possible abuse. The advisory says it may have been used alongside specific spam messages, but it does not say how many users may have been affected. WhatsApp Android Flaw Could Delete Local Files CVE-2026-102769 is a SQL injection flaw affecting WhatsApp for Android before version 2.26.35.74. SQL injection occurs when an app treats input as part of a database command rather than as data. According to the November advisory, file deletion required the recipient to tap an “order details” message. The advisory limits the possible damage to files stored locally by WhatsApp, not files across the device. The same flaw could also reveal one bit of information about the recipient’s chat database if they were online when the message arrived. That is a limited leak, not evidence that an attacker could read entire conversations. An external researcher reported the issue through Meta’s security reporting program. WhatsApp said it had seen no evidence of exploitation. CVE-2026-23871 affects WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for Android before version 2.26.17.4. The app did not fully check external media links in replies tied to Click to WhatsApp ads. A device could reveal its IP address when WhatsApp displayed the message in a chat. Unlike the file deletion flaw, the advisory does not describe a tap as necessary. An IP address is network information, not the contents of a chat. Cyber Security News previously covered a separate WhatsApp flaw involving Instagram Reels that also involved incomplete checks on media links. The two issues carry different CVE IDs and affect different app versions. CVE-2026-44908 affected how WhatsApp verified the identity of servers used by Meta AI’s Private Processing service . The flaw could have let someone positioned inside Meta’s infrastructure bypass a check meant to confirm that the server was running on trusted hardware. The advisory says the certificate would first have had to appear in a third-party record. All published certificates traced back to trusted hardware, which WhatsApp says confirms the flaw was not exploited. The certificate fix arrived in WhatsApp 2.26.24.72 for iOS, 2.26.23.74 for Android, and 2.26.23.72 for Mac. WhatsApp Business received fixes in 2.26.23.72 for iOS and 2.26.23.70 for Android. Users should install the latest available version from their official app store and check WhatsApp Business separately if they use both apps. The WhatsApp Security Advisories page notes that app store release notes may not list every security fix. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. View Details!
